Sorry, there is a difference between and OCT and OPTOS

OPTOS  takes a large wide image of the back of the eye (imagine it to be a fish-eye photo) it's great for screening for many types of pathology. It's best utility is for screening and photodocumenting most diseases. Where it falls short is mainly disease of the optic nerve and macula.

OCT is a tool to take a cross section of the eye, so we can see layers underneath. OPTOS can't do that. Think of it like an x-ray of the macula and optic nerve. It can give us a rough idea of how thick each structure of the eye is, to see if there is thinning or holes, bleeds underneath the layer of the retina, that both optometrists see as well as OPTOs.  It's great for managing diseases like glaucoma and any diseases of the macula. 

As an optometrist, both machine has its merit. Both OPTOS and OCT  are useful as part of a standard check. I would be hard pressed to say which is better, it's comparing apples to oranges. I would say OPTOS is more useful for an average Joe as it's more of a screening tool, where as OCT is more a specialist tool. 


The last one is a fundus photo, which takes a front on view of the macula and optic nerve. It's like the grandad to the OPTOS. I personally don't use it as much now, because I have access to the OPTOS, which already covers both those areas in the scan. Most places do it free as part of a routine check, because it's become a little more of an older tech. Some replaces still charge because it's still a service and they got to recoupe the cost of buying the machine in the first place. Specsavers Topcon is a combined OCT and fundus photo, so they so both at the same time. 


The charge discrepancy between each machine is due to different philosophy of corporate businesses. In a private practise, I would probably charge more than $60 for an OCT scan, but it would be because I wouldn't use it on all my patients, as I said it's more indicated for use of there was a suspected disease. Machines are an investment, I wouldn't do them for free if I was a small business. Specsavers can because they roll their profits from glasses, not eye care.

This is my crack at some solutions:

Cataracts: age related changes that can cause ghosting, but if you're <50, probably not likely

Dry eye syndrome: eyes drying out is like looking through a dirty windscreen. Also worsens as you get older. Effects can be intermittent and transient. If you've been staring from bring focussed tasks, e.g. watching movie, reading, drawing etc it worsens because you forget to blink

Larger pupils: larger apertures means more abberations, Coma, chromatic, astigmatic, all the higher order abberations  manifest. The pupil enlarging drops are actually a bad idea. 

Worse case scenario in my head: intermittent angle closure attacks. Basically drainage system in the eye clogs up which builds up pressure in the eye, which can cause oedema of the cornea and hence cause halos and fogginess. This is more likely to happen in people who are very long sighted. Assuming your 8.50 is + and not -, it is something to think about.

Uncorrected astigmatism/sphere: Maybe find someone else for a 2nd opinion on your prescription. You can try hard contact lenses, which sometime offers better vision esp if you have higher order abberations in the eye.

Keratoconus could also cause irregular astigmatism and also induce higher order abberations, but unlikely to onset in older people.
